edit: @AlmightyHarbinger, read the "What is Bitcoin?" text in the sidebar to the right if you haven't already.

One important thing that the other commenters haven't yet addressed is about how your conception of Bitcoin so far isn't completely right. I'm not going to go into too much detail, but this should help. You should also go to https://bitcoin.org and read as much as you need to get a general idea of how bitcoin works - you really need to read the FAQ and other documents (because Bitcoin is probably very different from anything you already know about, and your preexisting money ideas can lead to much confusion).

Bitcoin is not a company. There is no Bitcoin CEO (except for users jokingly named @Bitcoin_CEO or similar), nothing like that. Bitcoin is a technology. Your "how to create an account" questions is something like "how can I make an internet account", or "how can I get a 3G account for my phone" - a question that doesn't fit with the technology. While initially it may be easier to understand Bitcoin as "the money of the internet", in reality it is something more like "the internet of money" - it has tremendous potential.

Basically, the Bitcoin technology is built around the transfer of tokens (called bitcoin(s)) through a distributed, P2P ledger that anybody can download and inspect. While this has tremendous potential, currently the primary use of these tokens is as a store of value. A bitcoin has value because enough people agree that it is worth something to them (just like why the USD is worth something, for example). It's basically it's own currency, just like the USD or Euro, or whatever. Why people think it's worth something is a little more than what I'm going to go into, but currently enough people think it's worth something for one bitcoin to be worth around $280.

Continuing the bitcoin-internet analogy, there is no direct way to change USD that you have directly into bitcoin, just as it's impossible for the average internet user to upload something directly to the internet all by themselves. As the internet user needs a browser and a website, the Bitcoin user needs a special app (called a "wallet") and an exchange. The exchange converts your currency into Bitcoin or vice versa by matching you up with someone else (there are different types and many exchanges). The wallet app stores your bitcoin (note: all that's really needed to "store" bitcoin is a string of characters, so you can also store some or all of their bitcoin in paper - a "paper wallet", but a wallet app makes it easier to manage).

So, basically, in order to get some bitcoin, you'll need to choose a wallet and an exchange. A word of warning: due to the technological nature of Bitcoin, there are a lot of scams, so beware. For a wallet, bitcoin.org has a great page with pros and cons for different apps. Coinbase is a good place for beginners to get started, but you should be aware that you must share a lot of personal info and they track what you do with your bitcoin. If you really want good privacy, you can use another exchange like LocalBitcoins.com (see comment by @N2theoah) to get your bitcoin, and you can use a "tumbler" and other techniques to mix it up even more.

With any luck that writeup will help some. Sorry if it's not that coherent - it was just somethign of a collection of things that I thought you should know. And I'm sure there's some that I've missed.

For your specific questions:

How can you take money from it?

You can get traditional currencies (read: USD, etc.) through an exchange, but you can also spend bitcoin at certain websites/locations. Spending bitcoin is generally better than converting it to another currency to spend.

Is there a way to pay and put money on it without being tracked by anyone?

Bitcoin is both anonymous and not anonymous. Read the "Bitcoin is not anonymous" section on this page for a brief description, and look further if you don't understand. Import note about anonymity: every single transaction that is ever confirmed in the Bitcoin network is put on the public record, where anybody can see it. However, all this transaction displays is lots of letters and numbers, unless somehow those certain letters and numbers are connected to you in real life. If you don't connect your real life identity to your addresses (read: where you store you bitcoin), nobody can tell who owns them and who is spending them, but they can sometimes tell what is being done with them. If one of your addresses is associated with your real identity, it could potentially reveal all of your bitcoin records - who sent you money, how much you have, where you've spent it, etc. Basically, Bitcoin can be anywhere from very anonymous to very non-anonymous, depending on how you use it.

What about the fees?

If you don't want, you don't have to pay any fees. However, fees are often included - they will (often) decrease the confirmation time of your transaction, and they help miner (look up miners). Fees are usually around 0.0001 bitcoin, but you can set them to whatever you want.

Important last note: Make sure you have at least a general understanding of how the Bitcoin network before you put too much money into it.

And good luck! Hopefully my wall of text isn't too daunting or confusing or anything. Please ask questions if you have any, and other users, please correct/improve what I've said.
